prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "UNION PACIFIC CORP" (ticker UNP), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "UNP", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Union Pacific Corporation
markets: Bulk rail freight (grain and grain products, fertilizer, food and refrigerated, coal and renewables)
Industrial rail freight (industrial chemicals and plastics, metals and minerals, forest products, energy and specialized markets)
Premium rail freight (domestic and international intermodal containers and finished automotive vehicles)
Cross-border U.S.-Mexico rail freight (the only railroad serving all six major Mexico gateways)

mission.statement: Build America for all generations by connecting our nation's businesses and communities to each other and the world.
mission.source: Union Pacific website, Company Overview page (published as its Vision; its Purpose reads: "The people of Union Pacific deliver North America's safest, most reliable and most efficient supply chain solutions.")
mission.plain: Union Pacific wants to keep America's economy moving by carrying goods safely and reliably between businesses, towns and the rest of the world.

about.plain: Union Pacific runs one of the biggest freight railroads in America. Its trains carry things like grain, chemicals, coal, cars and shipping containers across 23 western states on about 32,900 miles of track. It owns the tracks, the locomotives and the yards, and companies pay it to move their goods. It also connects to Mexico and Canada and to ports on the West Coast and Gulf Coast.
about.customers: About 10,000 businesses such as farmers and grain companies, chemical and plastics makers, carmakers, steel and building-material firms, power plants and shipping companies.
about.everyday: Many of the boxes from online orders, the cars at dealerships and the wheat in your bread rode on a Union Pacific train at some point.

money.plain: chemicals, plastics, metals, rock, lumber and energy products (share of H1 2026 operating revenue)
grain, fertilizer, food, coal and renewable fuels (share of H1 2026 operating revenue)
intermodal shipping containers and new cars and trucks (share of H1 2026 operating revenue)
subsidiary services, accessorial charges and real-estate leases (share of H1 2026 operating revenue)

money.part: Transcontinental railroad via Norfolk Southern merger
money.plain: proposed acquisition of Norfolk Southern (1 UNP share plus $88.82 cash per NS share) to create the first coast-to-coast U.S. railroad; under STB review

result.summary: Union Pacific has a wide, durable moat: its 32,889-mile network of rights-of-way in the western U.S. could not be rebuilt today, and in most of its territory it shares the market only with BNSF, a classic efficient-scale duopoly. Rail moves heavy freight over long distances far more cheaply than trucks, which, together with industry-leading efficiency (59.8% operating ratio in 2025), gives it steady pricing power, though trucks cap prices on shorter and time-sensitive freight.

pricingPower.evidence: Union Pacific credits 'core pricing gains' for revenue growth year after year; in 2025 freight revenue excluding fuel surcharge rose 3% on only 1% more carloads, operating income margin held about 40% (9,846 of 24,510 $M), and its 2026 outlook affirms 'pricing dollars in excess of inflation dollars' while Q2 2026 carloads still grew 2%.

moats.evidence: The 160-year-old Union Pacific name is well known, but shippers choose railroads on route, price and service rather than brand.

Plants, mines, grain elevators and warehouses built on a Union Pacific line are often served by only one railroad, so switching means trucking or relocating; reciprocal-switching rules and truck competition limit this.

Each added customer, terminal and gateway (all six major Mexico gateways, West Coast and Gulf ports, interchanges with eastern railroads) makes the network more useful and denser traffic lowers unit costs, though this is more density economics than a pure network effect.

With $24.5B of 2025 revenue, the largest of any U.S. railroad, and the industry's lowest operating ratio (59.8% vs about 64-68% at NSC, CSX and BNSF), it moves bulk freight long distances at far lower cost than trucks.
The western U.S. rail market supports only two Class I networks (Union Pacific and BNSF); a new entrant could never earn a return on building a parallel network.
Union Pacific is the incumbent and its precision-scheduled model is used by all major railroads.

Under CEO Jim Vena it set records in 2025 for freight car velocity (225 daily miles, +8%), terminal dwell (20.9 hours, -8%) and workforce productivity (1,132 car miles per employee, +7%), but these operating practices can be copied by rivals over time.
It owns 32,889 route miles of rights-of-way across 23 states, land corridors through cities and mountain passes that could not be assembled again today.

customers.evidence: About 10,000 customers stay for decades because many facilities are rail-served only by Union Pacific, and 2025 service metrics hit records, but shipper groups often complain about rates and past service problems and many oppose the Norfolk Southern merger before the STB; no public NPS is disclosed.

talent.evidence: Pay is high (median employee compensation $107,889 in 2025) and retention was 89% in 2025, but about 83% of the workforce is unionized, headcount has been cut (average 29,287 employees in 2025) and it is not usually on top employer rankings.

product.evidence: Its network is the most extensive in the western U.S. and it posted the best efficiency of any U.S. Class I railroad in 2025 (59.8% operating ratio) with record velocity, dwell and an industry-leading personal-injury rate, though BNSF offers a closely comparable western network.

competitors.name: BNSF Railway (Burlington Northern Santa Fe, LLC; owned by Berkshire Hathaway)
competitors.note: The other western Class I railroad; head-to-head in intermodal, grain, coal, chemicals and Mexico/West Coast traffic. Files 10-K reports as debt issuer but has no listed stock.

competitors.name: CPKC (Canadian Pacific Kansas City Limited)
competitors.note: Competes for U.S.-Mexico cross-border, Midwest grain and Gulf chemicals traffic with its single-line Canada-U.S.-Mexico network.

competitors.name: Canadian National Railway Company
competitors.note: Competes for Midwest and Gulf chemicals, forest products and Chicago-Gulf traffic.

competitors.name: Norfolk Southern Corporation
competitors.note: Eastern railroad and interchange partner; Union Pacific has agreed to acquire it, pending STB approval.

competitors.name: CSX Corporation
competitors.note: Eastern railroad; competes indirectly via BNSF-CSX interline partnerships and for eastern-bound transcontinental freight.

competitors.name: J.B. Hunt Transport Services, Inc.
competitors.note: Largest intermodal marketer (partnered mainly with BNSF) and a truckload carrier competing for domestic container freight.

competitors.name: Knight-Swift Transportation Holdings Inc.
competitors.note: Largest U.S. truckload carrier; trucks compete for intermodal, automotive and industrial freight.

competitors.name: Schneider National, Inc.
competitors.note: Truckload and intermodal carrier competing for long-haul freight.

competitors.name: Werner Enterprises, Inc.
competitors.note: Truckload carrier including U.S.-Mexico cross-border trucking.

competitors.name: Hub Group, Inc.
competitors.note: Intermodal marketer and trucking firm that can shift container volume between railroads and trucks.

competitors.name: Kirby Corporation
competitors.note: Inland barge operator competing for chemicals and petrochemicals along the Gulf and Mississippi.

competitors.name: American Commercial Barge Line
competitors.note: Private Mississippi River barge operator competing for grain export traffic.

competitors.name: Grupo México (Ferromex)
competitors.note: Mexican railroad and partner at border gateways; competes for routing of Mexico freight.

estimates.name: BNSF Railway (Burlington Northern Santa Fe, LLC)

marketShare.market: Revenue of the four largest U.S. Class I railroads (UNP, BNSF, CSX, NSC; calculated from each company's reported FY2025 revenue)

threats: Regulatory and integration risk in the proposed Norfolk Southern acquisition: STB comments are due Nov 18, 2026 and final briefs May 28, 2027; Union Pacific owes a $2.5 billion fee if the deal fails on regulatory grounds, and conditions imposed could weaken returns.
Shipper and rival opposition (BNSF and shipper groups) could lead the STB to impose reciprocal switching, trackage rights or other access conditions that erode its captive-shipper pricing.
Trucking competition, especially if autonomous or electric trucks lower long-haul truck costs, and soft truck rates that pull intermodal freight off rail.
Long-term decline of coal volumes and exposure to cyclical industrial, housing and agricultural markets.
Trade and tariff policy affecting U.S.-Mexico cross-border and West Coast import traffic, where it is a leading carrier.
Labor relations: about 83% of employees are represented by 13 major rail unions, and crew-size or national bargaining outcomes could raise costs.
A major derailment or hazardous-materials accident (like Norfolk Southern's 2023 East Palestine incident) could bring large costs and new safety regulation.

ceo.name: Jim Vena
ceo.background: 40+ year railroader who began as a brakeman at Canadian National and rose to CN EVP and COO (2013-2016), then Union Pacific COO (2019-2020); B.Sc. in mathematics and chemistry, University of Alberta; Advanced Graduate Diploma in Management, Athabasca University

c1.evidence: Union Pacific leads a mature industry: U.S. freight rail is over 150 years old and its revenue was $24,875M in 2022 versus $24,510M in 2025.

c2.evidence: Shippers choose it because its 32,889-mile western network often is the only (or one of two) railroads reaching their plant, port or Mexico gateway at far lower cost than trucks, an advantage that cannot be copied and should last decades.

c3.evidence: The Union Pacific name and shield are widely recognised in the U.S. and it is the largest U.S. railroad by revenue, but it shares leadership with BNSF and shippers rarely recommend railroads enthusiastically.

c4.evidence: Its vision to 'Build America for all generations' is historic and meaningful, but management messaging centres on operating ratio, EPS growth targets and shareholder returns.

c6.evidence: “big, historic, trains, industrial”; the impression is mostly neutral to positive (the railroad that 'built America'), mixed with complaints about blocked crossings, rates and service from shippers and communities.

c7.evidence: The U.S. freight market is huge but rail volumes are roughly flat (carloads +1% in 2025); nearshoring to Mexico and truck-to-rail conversion are the main secular tailwinds.

c8.evidence: The proposed Norfolk Southern merger would create the first U.S. transcontinental railroad and open conversion of eastern long-haul truck freight, but outside rail its expansion options are limited.

m1.evidence: Jim Vena has a clear vision of a coast-to-coast single-line railroad that wins freight from trucks, pursued through the Norfolk Southern deal, though he is mainly an operations-focused executive.

m2.evidence: Vena is a hired CEO, but as a 40-plus-year railroader who started as a brakeman he works like an owner and is pushing a transformational, long-term merger.

m4.evidence: He emphasises safety and service to customers (record 2025 safety and service metrics, 'we delivered what we promised our customers'), but headcount cuts and union friction temper a servant-leader image.

m5.evidence: Vena has instilled a disciplined precision-scheduled operating culture that set records in velocity and productivity, but it is about execution rather than inventing new products.

m6.evidence: Vena is a hands-on operator who began as a brakeman, ran operations at CN and Union Pacific, and holds a science degree in mathematics and chemistry.

m7.evidence: No major personal controversies are known, but there is little public evidence of a broader humanitarian mission beyond running a safe, efficient railroad.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Jim Vena at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Vena is known in the industry as a blunt, outspoken railroader, but he is not a widely known public personality.

m9.evidence: Since August 2023 he cut the operating ratio to 59.8% in 2025 with record velocity and safety, and raised diluted EPS from $10.45 (2023) to $11.98 (2025).

m10.evidence: Precision-scheduled railroading focuses on cost control (average employees fell to 29,287 in 2025), but there is no specific public frugality story.

c10.evidence: Its trains move food, fertilizer, cars, chemicals and imported goods for about 10,000 customers, indirectly benefiting millions of Americans, but it serves mainly the U.S. rather than the whole world.

p2.evidence: Running a safe 32,889-mile network that moves millions of carloads a year is very hard and vital to the U.S. economy and food supply.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in 4 of the last 5 years ($19,533M in 2020 to $24,510M in 2025) but fell in 2023 ($24,119M from $24,875M).

f2.evidence: Operating margin was 40.1% in 2020 and 40.2% in 2025, after peaking at 42.8% in 2021 and dipping to 37.7% in 2023, so margins have been flat.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive ($20,673M at June 30, 2026), but debt of $30,327M is large against $2,114M of cash and short-term investments, about 3.3 times 2025 operating cash flow of $9,290M.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $7,834M (2020) to $9,846M (2025) and operating cash flow from $8,540M to $9,290M, but both dipped in 2023.

v1.evidence: For many western routes it is the cheapest and only rail option, and its 59.8% operating ratio is the industry's best, but BNSF offers a closely comparable network for many shippers.

v2.evidence: Pay and benefits are good (median pay $107,889) but Union Pacific is not regularly on top employer rankings and has strained relations with some unions.

c5.evidence: If it vanished, grain farmers, chemical plants, carmakers, power plants and importers across the West would lose their cheapest way to move heavy goods, pushing millions of extra trucks onto highways and raising prices.
